newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's 1997/98 budget relies on tax revenue.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's 1997/98 budget relies on tax revenue.

text.p: Indonesia's draft budget for 1997/98 released on Monday focussed on tax income as the main source for its expenditure, shifting further from its traditional reliance on income from oil and gas.
President Suharto proposed an 11.6 percent rise in the 1997/98 budget (April-March) from 90.62 trillion rupiah ($38.4 billion) in the current 1996/97 budget.
The draft budget showed revenue from income and value-added taxes were set to finance more than half the country's expenditures of 101.09 trillion rupiah ($42.8 billion).

Revenue from income and value-added taxes were expected to rise 22.8 and 12.9 percent to 29.12 trillion rupiah ($12.3 billion) and 24.6 trillion rupiah ($10.4 billion), respectively, from the 1996/97 budget (April-March).
But the government said it has no plan to raise taxes.
"...this budget does not plan to raise tax rates," Coordinating Minister for Economics and Finance Saleh Afiff told a briefing ahead of President Suharto's 1997/98 budget address to parliament.
Afiff said the government would focus on improving tax administration and tax collection to increase revenue from income and value-added tax, currently at 10 percent.
Economists said the government was on track to reduce the role of oil and gas in the country's budget.

Indonesia's reliance on oil and gas revenues, which accounted to over 65 percent of government domestic revenues in 1984/85, has diminished and contributes only 17 percent to revenue in the new draft budget.
At the same time, income and value-added taxes have increased steadily to 61 percent of government income in 1997/98 from 30 percent a decade ago.
Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said the increase in income tax revenue would help boost non-oil revenue by 14.2 percent compared with the increase in oil income of 5.3 percent.
Mar'ie dismissed fears that the optimistic target for tax income could not be reached if the economy slowed down during an election year. General elections will be held on May 29.
Some analysts said the Indonesian economy had slowed in the past because of general elections.
Indonesian budget revenues are made up of two components, domestic revenues and development revenues.
Domestic income, consisting of oil and non-oil revenues, is expected to rise by 12.6 percent to 88.06 trillion rupiah ($37.3 billion), accounting for 87.11 percent of the budget.
Development revenues are foreign aid from countries grouped in the Consultative Group for Indonesia (CGI).

Their role was seen declining gradually, contributing only to 12.9 percent, or 13.03 trillion rupiah ($5.5 billion) of the 1997/98 budget against 15.7 percent some 10 years ago, although in term of absolute numbers CGI funds have risen steadily.

Afiff said the 1997/98 budget also reflected the government's commitment to import tariff cuts to meet tariff regulations set in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Free Trade Area (AFTA) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC).
Revenue from import duties was set to decline to 3.32 trillion rupiah ($1.4 billion) from 3.45 trillion rupiah ($1.46 billion) in the 1996/97 budget.
